Series::log_softmax¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::log_softmax(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

log_softmax() is the logarithm of softmax(), computed as one fused operation so it never returns -inf for a finite input:

log_softmax(x)_i = x_i - log( sum_j exp(x_j) )
                 = x_i - logsumexp(x)

The dim argument chooses which axis is normalized; every other axis is left alone. On a [batch, classes] matrix, log_softmax(1) produces one row of log probabilities per example.

It exists as its own method — rather than leaving you to write x.softmax(dim).log() — for two reasons:

  • Stability. softmax() can legitimately underflow a small probability to exactly 0, and log(0) is -inf. log_softmax() subtracts logsumexp(x) from the raw scores instead, so every output is a finite real number.

  • Cost and gradient quality. The fused form skips a division and an exponential-then-logarithm round trip, and its backward is simpler and better conditioned.

This is the function a classification loss should be built on: cross-entropy for a one-hot target t is just -(t * log_softmax(x)).sum(dim).

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis to normalize over. Negative values count from the end. Must refer to a real axis; an out-of-range dim raises. There is no whole-series overload.

Returns¶

Series Log probabilities, the same shape and dtype as the input. Each value is <= 0; exp() of the result along dim sums to 1.

Gradient¶

log_softmax() is differentiable. With p = softmax(x) and an upstream sensitivity g, the backward along dim is

dx_i = g_i - p_i * sum_j g_j

For the cross-entropy case L = -(t * log_softmax(x)).sum(dim) with a probability vector t (sum 1), this collapses to the well-known

dL/dx = softmax(x) - t

— the prediction minus the target, with no softmax Jacobian to form explicitly.

Examples¶

Example 1. Row-wise log probabilities.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 2.0, 3.0},
    {1.0, 1.0, 1.0},
});

std::cout << scores.log_softmax(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-2.407606, -1.407606, -0.40760596],
  [-1.0986123, -1.0986123, -1.0986123]]

exp() of each row sums to 1; the uniform second row is log(1/3) = -1.0986 three times.

Example 2. Where it beats softmax().log().

auto z = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1000.0});

std::cout << "log(softmax(z)) = " << z.softmax(0).log();
std::cout << "log_softmax(z)  = " << z.log_softmax(0);

Output¶

log(softmax(z)) = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-inf, 0]
log_softmax(z)  = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1000, 0]

softmax([0, 1000]) underflows the first probability to 0, so its log is -inf. log_softmax keeps the exact value 0 - 1000 = -1000.

Example 3. Negative dim.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 2.0, 3.0},
    {1.0, 1.0, 1.0},
});

std::cout << scores.log_softmax(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-2.407606, -1.407606, -0.40760596],
  [-1.0986123, -1.0986123, -1.0986123]]

Example 4. Cross-entropy gradient is softmax(x) - target.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto target = pluss::make_series({{0.0, 1.0, 0.0}});   // class 1
auto loss = x.log_softmax(1).mul(target).sum().neg();
loss.reverse();

std::cout << "loss=" << loss.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL/dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

loss=1.40761
dL/dx=pluss::Series(shape=[1,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.090030573, -0.75527153, 0.66524096]]

The gradient is softmax(x) - target = [0.0900, 0.2447 - 1, 0.6652], and the loss is -log_softmax(x)_1 = 1.4076.

Example 5. An out-of-range dim is rejected.

try {
  pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}}).log_softmax(5);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

reduce: dim out of range

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • dim is required; there is no whole-series overload.

  • Prefer log_softmax(x) to softmax(x).log() in every case — it is finite where the latter is -inf, and it is cheaper.

  • The output is not a probability distribution; it is the log of one. exp(log_softmax(x)) recovers the probabilities.

  • Only score differences matter (a constant per-lane offset is invisible), exactly as for softmax().

Summary¶

log_softmax(dim) is the fused, finite log(softmax(x)):

  • x_i - logsumexp(x) along dim

  • never -inf for finite input; cheaper than softmax().log()

  • differentiable, backward g_i - p_i * sum g; cross-entropy gradient is softmax(x) - target

  • the right building block for a classification loss

See Also¶

  • Series::softmax: the distribution itself.

  • Series::logsumexp: the log sum exp term subtracted here.

  • Series::logcumsumexp: the running-prefix version of that term.

  • Series::nan_to_num: a blunt way to patch -inf after the fact — log_softmax avoids needing it.
